lesson.title: From Slope Map to Skyline: Building f from f'
lesson.summary: Given only the graph of f', its sign pattern and its zeros, you can reconstruct the essential shape of f, its rises, falls, peaks, valleys, and bends, without ever being told a formula for f.
lesson.body:
Suppose you are shown the graph of f' with no formula attached, and asked to sketch f. The method is a direct application of the f-to-f' correspondence, just run backward: wherever the f' graph sits above the x-axis, f is increasing; wherever it sits below, f is decreasing; every zero crossing of f' is a candidate local extremum of f, classified by which direction the crossing goes; and wherever f' itself is rising, f is concave up, while wherever f' is falling, f is concave down, with inflection points of f sitting at the peaks and valleys of the f' graph.

Suppose the graph of f' shows the following behavior: negative for all x less than -1, crossing zero at x = -1 heading upward, positive on the interval from -1 to 2, crossing zero at x = 2 heading downward, and negative again for all x greater than 2. From this description alone, without any formula, f must be decreasing on (-infinity, -1), reach a local minimum at x = -1 (since f' crosses from negative to positive there), increase on (-1, 2), reach a local maximum at x = 2 (since f' crosses from positive to negative there), and decrease again on (2, infinity).

To get the concavity of f, look at where the f' graph itself is rising and falling, since that is the sign of f''. A downward-opening parabola shape for f' (negative, rising to a positive hump, falling back to negative) rises on its left half and falls on its right half, with its own peak sitting midway between its two zeros. Between the zeros at x = -1 and x = 2, the midpoint is x = 1/2, so f' is increasing on (-infinity, 1/2) and decreasing on (1/2, infinity). That means f is concave up on (-infinity, 1/2) and concave down on (1/2, infinity), with an inflection point at x = 1/2, sitting inside the increasing stretch of f between its local min and local max.

As a check, this sign pattern is exactly produced by f'(x) = -x^2 + x + 2 = -(x - 2)(x + 1), and one antiderivative is f(x) = -x^3/3 + x^2/2 + 2x. Differentiating confirms f'(x) = -x^2 + x + 2, matching the description. Computing key values: f(-1) = 1/3 + 1/2 - 2 = -7/6, the local minimum; f(2) = -8/3 + 2 + 4 = 10/3, the local maximum; and f(1/2) = -1/24 + 3/24 + 1 = 13/12, the inflection point, which does sit between -7/6 and 10/3 as it should, since f is increasing through that whole stretch. Checking end behavior, the dominant term -x^3/3 sends f to positive infinity as x approaches negative infinity and to negative infinity as x approaches positive infinity.

Assembling all of it: the graph of f comes up from positive infinity on the far left, falls to a local minimum of -7/6 at x = -1, rises through an inflection point at (1/2, 13/12) where it switches from bending upward to bending downward, continues rising to a local maximum of 10/3 at x = 2, then falls without bound as x increases from there. None of that shape required knowing the formula in advance; every piece of it came directly from reading the sign pattern and turning points of f'.
